akikiie.name: Akikiie
akikiie.html:
Aki, Silveh on Discord, built the house the Dusk era lived in: the first message in the entire officer-chat archive is him setting up the Ninjas server in April 2020, gated roles and class channels and all. He was a Ninjas officer, a warrior with fifty-eight raid nights, and a steady tactical voice through the AQ progression, explaining Huhuran nature-resistance splits in paragraphs while others argued in fragments.

His guild life ended on a single pull. On 17 September 2020 he pulled at the Ahn'Qiraj entrance with nobody ready. The world buffs died, Ulfhild rage-quit, and three days of officer warfare followed. Aki owned it completely: "I'll happily apologise and take the blame for it. It's not my intent to hide from it." Then he asked the question underneath the whole affair, whether he actually enjoyed a game where a single wipe could ruin forty people's evening. He decided he didn't, and left within the week. The archive remembers him as the architect of the guild's home and the first casualty of its seriousness.

suspected alts — co-absence analysis.name: Suspected alts — co-absence analysis
suspected alts — co-absence analysis.html:
Generated 2026-07-30 from canonical Warcraft Logs rosters. Method (Anders's idea): for each low-session character that joined two or more months into the archive, find high-attendance mains who were active in the same window and lineages but absent from essentially every raid the candidate alt attended (at most one shared session, which allows a mid-raid character swap — Artimis/Lege share three sessions that way). The score is how improbable the main's absences are given their normal attendance rate; higher is more suspicious.

None of these are in `alts.json` yet — promote a pair only after confirmation (a Discord statement, a workbook comment, or Anders/participant memory). Validated confirmed pairs (Rocka→Rockafella, Yukikitsune→Glorya) show the same signature this analysis looks for.

- Isamu (Mage, 40 sessions) → Glorya: Anders tentatively remembers Isamu as Knut's mage alt (2026-07-30). The raid archive is compatible: Isamu and Glorya share no sessions. Keep this unconfirmed until Anders or Glorya can remove the uncertainty.

## Strong — name similarity plus co-absence

All four confirmed by Anders 2026-07-30 and promoted to `alts.json`: Devouboi→Devou, Hiltsey→Hilts, Steewie→Steewiee, Tsiko→Tsakimo.

## Medium — co-absence only, plausible

| Suspected alt | Candidate main | Signal | |---|---|---| | Holyhans (Paladin, 11n, Jun–Sep) | Dolleboy (Druid) | 0 shared at 0.68; Dolleboy also pairs with Powerhealer (Priest, 6n) at 0.73 — one main, possibly two alts | | Wetfarter (Hunter, 11n, Jun–Sep) | Amberlynreid (Rogue) | 0 shared at 0.68 | | Maevis (Mage, 12n, Jun–Oct) | Rangah (Hunter) | 0 shared at 0.63 | | Nonstickpan (Rogue, 10n, Jun–Oct) | Saltyhead (Rogue) | 0 shared at 0.68; same class weakens it | | Melic (Hunter, 16n, Apr–Sep) | Mysor (Rogue) | 1 shared at 0.59 | | Gallithian (Mage, 11n, May–Aug) | Exhopresso (Warrior) | 0 shared at 0.58 | | Darkranger (Hunter, 5n, May–Jun) | Divinestorm (Mage) | 0 shared at 0.56; small sample — but ask Divinestorm, it would be a fun detail |

## Weak or likely explained

- Namelessqt, Subroza, and Aggeeinn all pair with Crok in Oct–Dec windows — more likely Crok simply attended less that autumn than that he ran three alts; treat as noise unless confirmed. - Filippoberio pairs with Ragie statistically, but the Dusk officer chat treats Filippo as his own person ("Deltron and Filippo were benched") — rejected. - Mdsthesecond (Priest, 5n) — the name says "the second [character]" of someone; statistics point weakly at Priestå or Spaxi. The name alone makes it worth asking about. - Divinehealer (Priest, 8n, Oct–Feb) pairs with Glorya/Selephie at low confidence; Glorya's confirmed alt is the rogue Yukikitsune, so a second priest alt is unlikely. - Mikai (Rogue, 5n) pairs weakly with Amberlynreid; note the unresolved Mika/Mikadro/Mikasalord name cluster from the loot workbook.

Ask in the Dusk Discord or during participant interviews; check the workbook comment column for the main's name on the alt's loot rows; or search the officer chat for the alt's name. On confirmation, add to `alts.json` and note the evidence in `alts-evidence.md`.

antzi.name: Antzi
antzi.html:
Antzi ran the rogues — before the merger in Ninjas, after it in Dusk — and brought to the officer chat a philosophy he repeated until everyone could recite it: focus is respect. He didn't care if you came unbuffed; he cared if you wasted thirty-nine other people's evening. "I play this game for the community," he wrote in one of the autumn's better manifestos, and meant it literally — his rogues never once made loot drama, a record he defended with visible pride.

His temper was the cost of the conviction. The September crises pulled him into shouting matches with Divinestorm ("no brain pull"), with Rockafella ("stick to ur lock"), and into the Band of Accuria blowup where he heard himself called stupid and demanded it never happen again. But the record consistently shows the anger pointing somewhere real: at carelessness, at gift-loot logic, at anything that treated the raid's time as free. When he admitted he'd talked his rogues out of quitting "with arguments I don't even believe," it was the most honest sentence of the whole autumn.

artimis.name: Artimis
artimis.html:
Artimis joined Dejvid's young guild in the autumn of 2019 and was soon running it in practice — formally from February 2020, when Dejvid handed over the reins. He ran it the way he ran everything: with spreadsheets. The attendance workbook was his. So was the loot log, started 2020-03-29 with a plea that class leaders post every drop, and the raider-rank system with its promise that showing up mattered. Most of it outlived his tenure. As a hunter he negotiated the early Rhok'delar queue one player at a time, then finished his own bow around 11 November 2019. As an alchemist he ran a one-man consumables service, mailing flasks to tanks and crafting anything anyone needed. His priest alt Lege healed whenever the roster came up short.

He gave the guild away twice. In early 2020 he offered the leadership to Kodf, who declined; in August 2020, minutes after a Nefarian kill, he told the raid that Divinestorm would be the new Guild Master and thanked everyone for their trust — handing over the guild mid-raid, in the same breath as a boss kill. He stayed on as the institutional memory: teaching the spreadsheets, mediating disputes, and writing the rules other people argued about.

The governing instinct underneath the spreadsheets was collective. In April, while the mage class argued over its leader, he refused to act as a "solo ruler" and put the decision to the officers. That habit made him slower than a dictator and harder to blame alone, which was usually the point.

December 2020 made him the story's protagonist against his will. When the Ascension merge cut the roster to twenty and the promises of the raider-rank system stopped being honoured, Artimis wrote a five-point proposal (raiders before members, whole-lockout spots, collective bench decisions) and asked members to strike. He himself had been benched from every single Four Horsemen attempt. The strike never happened; the guild dissolved into Ascension two days later. He kept raiding into 2021, kept the records, and years later those records became this site.

The bench had already pushed him into a second raid life. From November he guest-healed external gold-bid raids on Lege because the priest had hit the guild's alt-loot ceiling. That ended in the final days of December, when his child arrived and weekend raid invitations stopped fitting the life around them.

banamahs.name: Banamahs
banamahs.html:
Banamahs led the Thursday mages and thought about guilds the way an economist thinks about fisheries: the resource is your members' time and goodwill, and every scuffed raid overfishes it. "Longevity is the key to this game," he wrote in September, "but if you burn resources too quickly, people quit." He said it about continuation raids, about split-run chaos, about consumable costs — and the autumn kept proving him right.

He was the calm half of the Ninjas bloc: building loot-overview spreadsheets other class leaders copied, absorbing a mage exodus (three top-geared mages gone in a week) with recruitment plans instead of drama, and cutting through the era's worst arguments with lines like "this wasn't a case of afk players — we were not ready to pull." His tribute to Ulfhild doubles as his own epitaph for the era: if everyone pumped that hard, the raid would take forty-five minutes.

boxya.name: Boxya
boxya.html: Boxya's guild career is a two-act comedy of timing. Recruited by Luivi as a friend of Wandolina, he signed up for a September raid, never showed, and left the guild the next day. Yet by December he was back and suddenly indispensable: picked as one of Dusk's two protected tanks in the Ascension merge — and then he left again, days later, forcing Ragie into the spot. Two departures, both at the worst possible moment; the tank crisis that drove the December merge has his fingerprints on it.

celed.name: Celed
celed.html: Celed was a rogue from the Ninjas line who held the class-leader seat as a stand-in when Antzi's work schedule bit, and gave it back with the most graceful resignation in the record: "Antzi wants to replace me! We talked about it so much and this is our decision... he knows so much about the game. I'll help going forward." No drama, no politics, a 72-raid resume, and a healer-parse joke at his expense that followed him around one autumn week ("95 parse is worthy of some loot, actually"). The guild ran on its arguers; it also ran on people like Celed, who mostly just showed up and played well.

crok.name: Crok
crok.html: Crok was a mage with 164 raids in the logs — one of the most-attended players in the whole archive — and the pragmatist in the officer chat. When rosters ran short he suggested filling with pugs and recruiting the good ones ("worked in the past"); when December's crisis meetings ran hot he stayed practical. His DM thread with Anders spans the guild's whole life, from a February 2020 recruit conversation to three days after the Kel'Thuzad kill. He farmed venom sacks on the night crew, carried the Ring of Spiritual Fervor out of the 12-wipe Horsemen night, and made the jump to Ascension with the rest. During migration week he also relayed alchemy materials between Rockafella and the benched Artimis, keeping the consumables line moving while the guild changed names.

deliz.name: Deliz
deliz.html:
Deliz was a healer, one of the guild's Norwegian core, and the story's first fairness casualty. In February 2020, a year before anyone had heard of Ascension, he quit WoW over how healers were treated: excluded from best-in-slot rolls while the damage dealers geared, with a disputed Ragnaros neck as the concrete grievance. His exit put a question on the table that the guild never fully answered, and that returned in every later crisis: what does the raid owe the people who keep it alive but never top a meter?

His friendship with Anders long outlasted his raiding. The messages run from 2019 to 2025 — game recommendations, life updates, and the occasional piece of guild news from the outside, including the December 2020 note that Chris had deleted the old WoW Classic Discord. In the story of Sleep he is the early warning: the guild's kindest era already contained the argument that would end it.

devou.name: Devou
devou.html: Devou was Ascension's warrior officer and the other half of the December negotiation. From the Dusk side of the record he appears as a fair counterpart: the one who offered his own raid spot to a benched Dusk hunter on the first joint night ("thank Devou," Divinestorm insisted, "for understanding how much we wanted a 3rd hunter spot"), and the firm no when a fourth hunter spot was floated. Ascension wanted to stay Ascension and absorb Dusk; he said so openly from day one, which is more than most mergers get. The Ascension side of this story — the KT week, the January era — is still waiting for his version.

divinestorm.name: Divinestorm
divinestorm.html:
Divinestorm arrived as a mage in February 2020 and ended the year running the guild. The climb started with an April challenge to mage leader Proctologist. Divinestorm took his case to Artimis, and Rockafella backed him as the person who should have led from the start. The officers made the change. Next came the Dusk channel structure and the loot doctrine, which measured effort through attendance and preparation while leaving the final word with the council. By 2 August he had 91 raids behind him and became guild master. The officer chat shows him everywhere. He ran the idol economy item by item, defended benched players one day ("we solved problems for the top raiders, but we haven't solved it for those we bench") and made hard calls the next ("I have no problem making hard calls if needed").

He was also the guild's shock absorber. September 2020 brought a crisis a week: a ninja pull, a rage-quit, an officer resigning live in the channel, a kick war that briefly cost the guild its own tank leader. Divinestorm mediated every one of them, often from work trips, and wrote the member-facing statements afterwards. When Naxxramas exposed the tank roster in December, he concluded overnight that the guild could not continue alone, opened talks with Ascension's officers, and eight days later led the mass migration, planned while everyone hearthed into the raid. The 15/15 Kel'Thuzad kill came four days after that, under his leadership.

The record keeps his personality intact. He bought poison sacs by the hundred and tracked idol distribution person by person. He defended a benched no-name because "the guy worked really hard farming sacs for us", then called himself "the mage who didn't understand hunter loot" while arbitrating a hunter loot fight. He was sworn at in officer chat and told to his face that the leadership was running the guild into the ground, and he answered with the same maddening evenness every time. That evenness is why people trusted him with the December decisions.

It also won people back. Tsakimo quit in July over the rogue loot system, spoke privately with Divinestorm, and returned for Dusk's first AQ40 night as the person updating the loot sheet.

Those decisions are the hard part of his file. The pivot to Ascension saved the raid; 15/15 in fourteen days is the proof. It also ended the guild as a thing of its own and cost it its most loyal bench. Divinestorm took the blame for a botched benching in the same breath as he claimed the authority to bench anyone, which suggests he understood the price better than anyone else at the time.

edomedo.name: Edomedo
edomedo.html: Edomedo was the tank-in-waiting whose exit changed everything. Groomed through November as the contingency ("we have a potential tank lined up"), he preferred tanking to DPS and said so. On the night of December 7th 2020 he told Divinestorm he was quitting the game — and that single conversation set off the chain reaction: no tanks for Four Horsemen, the overnight partnership with Ascension, the twenty-spot cut, and the end of Dusk nine days later. Few players this quiet ever moved a story this much.

exclus.name: Exclus
exclus.html:
Exclus came from the Nittedal group as a mage. His holy paladin alt Exclusafk joined a roster whose four paladin spots were all healers. The two characters account for nearly one hundred logged raids between them.

He was also a connector. On 23 October 2019 he vouched for Ragie as "a really good tank," bringing in the player who would anchor the guild's front line.

When Thepaladin lost access to his account, Exclusafk covered the class-leader job from 15 to 22 April 2020. Exclus declined the permanent seat because he was not playing enough, and Randyfist took over. A month later Ragie tried to recruit the paladin alt onto a warrior, creating a brief boundary fight between the tank and paladin leaders. Exclusafk kept raiding through September.

ferrua.name: Ferrua
ferrua.html:
Ferrua was a warlock from the Ninjas side with a talent for being the adult in the room. He is the officer whose loot judgment aged best ("turns out Ferrua was right not to give Mika the Rejuv Gem," Luivi conceded months later) and the one who ran healer loot on zero notice the day Orish quit. "Does this mean I decide healer loot today?" he asked. He did it well enough that nobody complained, which in this guild counts as a standing ovation.

His interventions were short and usually decisive: on rage-quitting ("imagine if ten people rage quit, we have no raid"), on second chances, and in defence of Divinestorm when criticism turned personal. He argued for diverse raid comps on principle. "Imagine if we only had warriors and paladins. That would suck."

fizzi.name: Fizzi
fizzi.html:
Fizzi was a warrior who treated raid rosters like an engineering problem. By late 2020 he was the Dusk officer doing the unglamorous math: how many hunter spots a merged raid could carry, which classes were oversubscribed, who could tank Four Horsemen if Boxya disappeared again (he kept Edomedo warm as the contingency). When the December merge happened, he was one of the two tanks Dusk protected in the first brutal cut. He had earned it; he'd tanked C'Thun with Glory just weeks earlier.

His philosophy was stated plainly in the December debates: comp plus parse — with limited spots you bring the players who perform, and "bench decisions… I have no problem making hard calls if needed." But the same person argued for alt-and-member loot parity in November, defended benched players' access to gear, and did the tedious work of maintaining signup tabs and week-three spreadsheets that fairness actually runs on.

He was in the first Four Horsemen kill and the Kel'Thuzad clear, and carried on into Ascension's farm era — one of the people whose December choices the story judges gently, because the archive shows how much thought went into them.

fnats.name: Fnats
fnats.html:
Fnats was Fredrik from Nittedal, a restoration druid, and the first voice in the whole archive: "Er du i queue?", sent from the launch-day line on 27 August 2019 while his druid was level 10. He and Anders had been gaming together long before Classic, and kept at it long after: League, Valorant, Tarkov, Halo, whatever was going that month.

In the guild he was one of the two best healers on the roster and the man who fought hardest to make healing loot fair. He spent two months trying to get the Rejuvenating Gem priority settled and eight days waiting for an answer about the healing-officer role. On 18 March 2020, Shakey won the first gem roll, Anders finally offered Fnats the officer role the same evening, and Fnats took an exam break from the game instead. He left without bitterness and with the most quoted line a guild leader ever received: "as guild leader, you unfortunately stand in the crossfire." His deeper argument outlived the night: the people deciding healer loot were people who would never play a healer.

galidia.name: Galidia
galidia.html:
Galidia was a warrior from the Nittedal circle and the recipient of the first loot award in the entire workbook: Bracelets of Wrath, Blackwing Lair, 25 March 2020, row one of the ledger everything on this site's loot pages descends from. He raided through the Sleep spring as one of the dependable middle of the roster, the kind of player the officer chat only mentions when a tank is needed on short notice ("I can ask Galidia or Naru to tank, they have the gear").

The friendship outlasted the guild by years. The same DM thread that covers raid signups in 2020 is, by 2025, Anders explaining index funds and stock picks. Nittedal threads don't really end; they just change topics.

glory.name: Glory
glory.html:
Glory joined in mid-February 2020, recruited almost by accident: Anders mistook him for someone else and had already mailed him a cloak before anyone caught the mix-up. He stayed for over 120 raids at 96% attendance. He was a protection warrior and a blacksmith good enough to forge Thepaladin's Sulfuron Hammer in March, then five of the six Radiant pieces for the Naxxramas frost-resistance push. By December 2020 he owned a completed Thunderfury, one of very few in the guild.

He asked for very little back. As early as March 2020 he was arguing for nothing more than a fair system, where effort at the bottom of the meters got the same respect as parses at the top. He tanked C'Thun for Dusk as late as November 12th. Then the December merge with Ascension cut the roster to twenty spots, and Glory never got a single Four Horsemen pull. Not one of the twelve wipes on December 13th. On the 14th, at 14:21, he told Anders the guild master had promised him a spot that evening; at 19:42 the Horsemen died on the night's first pull with forty other names in the log. He heard the strategy briefing from the bench.

The officers had reached a private verdict that same day: a year and a half of trial, not improved, not good enough. Nobody said it to his face. When he asked Anders directly who had blocked him, Anders refused to name names, and the answer stayed buried in the archive for five years. Anders had written his own strike letter that same morning, asking more or less the question Glory's whole December asked: what does a guild owe the loyal? Neither of them got an answer.

Two days later, on the evening the guild mass-migrated into Ascension, Glory left. "Better to go during the change," he said; the guild had been his home, and a spot every other week would have been enough to keep him. Within a week he was tanking Four Horsemen for another guild, in the deep Protection spec he had respecced to on the afternoon Dusk one-shot the fight without him. Invited back after the 15/15 clear, he declined; he couldn't abandon the people who had given him a spot. His last word in the archive, from 2022: not playing WoW any more, for now.

glorya.name: Glorya
glorya.html:
Glorya, Knut among the guild's Norwegians, was a priest healer whose name caused two years of clerical confusion with the warrior Glory, a coincidence the archive has to untangle on nearly every page. The two could hardly have had more different Decembers: while Glory watched the Four Horsemen progression from the bench, Glorya healed it. He is in the roster of the first kill on December 14th and stayed for the full Kel'Thuzad clear.

Dusk's healing was its export product, and Glorya was part of the core that made the merge attractive to Ascension in the first place. He was the kind of steady presence who shows up in the logs far more often than in the drama. When raids ran late or short-handed, Glorya arriving "potentially a little bit late" with Pnats was a recurring line in the healer logistics. His tribute video sits on Supplier's 2021 "Dusk list," between Shakey's and Carmelia's.

hedara.name: Hedara
hedara.html: Hedara was Ascension's druid officer, the second name Divinestorm gave Dusk when the December partnership formed. The archive holds less of him than his role deserves: a healer in the first Four Horsemen kill and the Kel'Thuzad clear, a short friendly DM with Anders about whether they'd met before ("You're from Norway, right? Your voice is familiar"), and a place in every joint-raid roster through the clear. Like Devou, he is a door this story hasn't opened yet — the Ascension officer chat from December would answer questions this archive can only pose.

henne.name: Henne
henne.html:
Henne (Linda) came over from the Ninjas side and was one of the voices that bridged the two cultures. Her place in the story is collateral damage from the strangest day of the Dusk era: on September 30th 2020, Jón Snjór was kicked without warning and used his alt's rank to kick Henne in retaliation before anyone could react. The protest gquits that followed nearly took the guild apart. Anders's first message to her that afternoon opens one of the archive's DM threads: let's find out what happened and find a fair solution.

She was restored along with everyone else once Divinestorm untangled the mess, and the incident forced the reform that outlived it: kick rights were restricted, and "if you don't have time to explain, you should not have time to kick people" became guild doctrine. Few players did less to deserve their place in the drama, which is why her name is on the reform.

jellopy.name: Jellopy
jellopy.html:
Jellopy was the guild's first rogue class leader, running the class through the Molten Core and Onyxia autumn of 2019 with a five-slot raider roster he picked himself. He also wired early Discord webhooks for Anders, part class leader and part guild tech support.

His 26 logged nights all predate Blackwing Lair. On 4 February 2020 he delegated the job plainly: "Kodf will act as CL and loot council." Three weeks later Anders asked whether the promotion should become permanent. "Yea for sure, promote the man!" Jellopy replied. He had hoped to do one last raid before announcing his own departure, but never found the time. Most guild history isn't drama. Sometimes the important people just log off.

knedlica.name: Knedlica
knedlica.html:
Knedlica was one of the hunters waiting for an Ancient Petrified Leaf in the guild's first winter. His gun was already stronger than Ravna's and Nereb's bows, so Artimis asked whether they could go first. Knedlica agreed, adding his own theorycraft about weapon speed and waiting for the tier pants that would solve his hit chance.

Real life pulled him away in spring 2020, when the pandemic and a local earthquake made raiding impossible. He asked to be moved to an inactive rank and hoped to return for a later phase. It was the kind of departure the early guild handled well: clear and without blame.

kodf.name: Kodf
kodf.html:
Kodf ran the rogues, and for a while he quietly ran much of the guild. Jellopy made him acting rogue leader on 4 February 2020 and endorsed the full promotion twenty days later. Kodf built the loot system his class became famous for, fair enough that months after he left officers were still wishing someone could "do Kodf's system." His officer-chat exchanges with Artimis in March 2020 are the guild's constitutional debates: hunters versus rogues on weapon priority, how much a member who shows up is owed, and whether kindness or performance should decide the marginal raid spot.

He was also the road not taken. When Artimis looked for a successor, Kodf got the first offer to take over Sleep, and he declined. In early July he was already rarely online. His final class-leader work included moving Ntekapaz to daggers and planning a seventh rogue spot. By 9 July he had left for Conviction; Lyvana followed by the 11th, while Kodf's alt remained behind. He left the way he did everything: tidily, with a handover, and he kept helping his old guildmates afterwards.

His fingerprints stayed on the guild long after his name left the roster: the rogue loot queues, the expectation that a class leader actually leads, and a small mystery he'd be amused by. The officers spent the autumn debating "another Kodf" and never quite found one.

kugel.name: Kugel
kugel.html:
Kugel was the original main tank, the warrior the guild built its first raids around. He recruited Thepaladin, who remembered him as the first person he got to know in Sleep, and received an early Binding of the Windseeker when handing a legendary component to your main tank seemed obviously right. Then, in January 2020, he simply stopped logging in. Thepaladin counted twenty-three days of silence before the officers began asking around. By February the main-tank vacancy was official, and in March Kugel was quietly removed after two months offline.

His disappearance shaped the guild twice over. It handed the tank mantle to Ragie and opened the gearing question that Glory, Zhena, and later Jón Snjór would each live through in turn. And the Binding that left with him became guild doctrine: from then on, legendary priority was tied to reliability and long-term commitment — a rule written, like most guild rules, in response to a specific disappointment. Nobody in the archive ever says where he went.

luivi.name: Luivi
luivi.html:
Luivi was the druid class leader whose one decision reshaped the whole story: in July 2020, Sleep offered him the guild-master seat. He turned it down (no time for it) and instead asked his contacts in Ninjas whether they'd consider merging. That conversation became Dusk. It's hard to name a more consequential "no" in the guild's history.

As a leader he ran the druids with visible pride ("Druids, the most civilized Class") and a warm, blunt style that survived translation from his native language into rapid-fire officer-chat English. In the Nayla saga he was the patient center, voting for a last warning while admitting the man exhausted him. When officer arguments overheated he was the one who kept perspective: no one was dying, the content was getting cleared, chill out a bit.

He raided everywhere: main raids on Luivi, fill-ins on his alt Vikka, off-tanking in cat spec when asked, venom-sack farm runs until he literally fell asleep at the keyboard mid-session (the officers renamed the voice channel "Sleepy Luivi" and tiptoed out). He became a Dusk officer in September, made the jump to Ascension in December, and stayed one of the last active voices in the old officer channel deep into 2021. In April he and Shakey also caught the stranger on Thepaladin's stolen account quitting Sleep, and warned the owner while it happened.

missdotty.name: Missdotty
missdotty.html:
Missdotty, Dotty for short and Decretum on Discord, was a warlock, the Thursday team's off-boss tank when a fight demanded one, and the officer chat's investigator-in-chief. When idols went missing from the guild bank pipeline, Dotty traced them mailbox by mailbox ("the investigator!"). When arguments ran to 150 messages, Dotty arrived late, sighed "99% shit, 1% information, as usual," and set up a poll. The Among Us jokes wrote themselves, and Dotty leaned in.

The record also holds a running comedy of mistaken identity: half the guild spent months assuming Missdotty was a woman, a discovery that cost Pnats a genuine crisis ("She's not?" / "I can be, if you want"). Behind the jokes sat a reliable officer, hardline in the Nayla debate, generous in the Tear queue, and the one who kept Discord's machinery of polls and roles and tags actually working.

nayla.name: Nayla
nayla.html:
Nayla was a feral druid and off-tank whose two years in the guild produced more officer-chat discussion than almost anyone else's. He was generous with his time, always available, always signed, and famously difficult to pin down: conversations relayed through him had a way of arriving changed, to the point where officers joked they needed screenshots.

The warning signs predated Dusk. In July 2020 an officer was already explaining a dispute with "Nayla has a feud with many people." The same week Nayla bought a Scarlet Kris from the guild bank, a small reminder that the ordinary guild machinery kept running around the conflict.

The autumn of 2020 is where his file thickens. An apparent ninja pull in AQ20 turned out, on investigation, to be a misunderstanding (he had been teleported onto the boss while trying to hearth out), but it landed on top of older friction and split the officers between removal and mercy. They debated for a night; one called his behavior toxic, another called him loyalty you can't buy. The verdict was one final chance, framed as a fresh start for the new guild. He lost his tank spot soon after, flirted with rerolling rogue, and was still being proposed for raider rank as late as October. Then on 25 November he left in a burst of drama, messaging guild members that their leader had committed a "last desperate act of evilness". What that act was, the archive still doesn't record. By December he had found a new guild and a new audience on the realm Discord.

The record is unusually rich on how people experienced him. His class leader defended him as "a soul whose intentions are good" in the same message as admitting he was exhausting. Officers learned to talk to him only in pairs, so there would be a witness. When he told one officer he had "lost his tanking spot", the officer who supposedly took it away had no idea what he was talking about — a small scene that explains his whole file.

And yet the guild kept almost keeping him. He survived a removal announcement, earned back a bench slot, and was seriously proposed for promotion six weeks before the end. Whatever his parting accusation meant, within two weeks he was raiding elsewhere, loudly himself on the realm Discord. His will to play was never the problem.

neptun.name: Neptun
neptun.html: Neptun was a mage in the December core, one of the names the officers refused to cut when the merge math got brutal ("we don't want to cut Neptun or Jumanzy or Electro — all three of them in a good raid team will perform very well"), and part of the first Four Horsemen kill and the Kel'Thuzad clear. The account is believed to have been played by Henriette from the Nittedal circle, which would make the December roster more Nittedal than anyone realised at the time. To be confirmed; the logs only know the character.

nereb.name: Nereb
nereb.html: Nereb was the third hunter in the rotation that defined December — the agreement by which he, Artimis and Zados took turns sitting out when the merged raid allowed the class only a few spots. He'd been there from the early days. In November 2019 Knedlica agreed that Nereb and Ravna, whose bows were weaker, should receive Rhok'delar leaves before him. Nereb was in the first Four Horsemen kill on the night both his rotation partners watched from outside. In the debates about hunter spots he was one of the three names even the hardliners agreed had to be protected: "Artimis is a special case, so is Zados and Nereb."

ntekapaz.name: Ntekapaz
ntekapaz.html:
Ntekapaz joined Sleep through Tsakimo and Carmelia on 28 June 2020. The rogue was only five days old but already attuned. He wanted a team worth staying with. When told that alts could receive loot before initiates, he objected once, then gave the line that explains why he fit: "I dont mind wasting a few gear runs in order to have a nice raidingteam."

Kodf moved him to daggers and funnelled the available drops his way, planning a seventh rogue spot even as he prepared to leave. Ntekapaz then became the clearest witness to the three-week Twx experiment. He reported the self-awarded tier pieces and challenged performance loot with the logs. His answer was always Kodf's round-robin system. Other rogues left. Ntekapaz stayed because he believed the problem could be fixed.

His warrior Malakor later joined the same November pug as Tsakimo and Artimis, proof that the friendships survived the loot revolt. He was also leveling the summon bot Ntekabot when the thread ends.

orish.name: Orish
orish.html:
Orish, Dan on Discord, was the Thursday raid's healing brain and the most quotable internal critic the guild ever had. He came over with Ninjas, built the healer loot plans item by item, and leveled three warlocks just to run summons for other people's world buffs. He defended his turf in prose that still crackles: anyone trying to snake healing loot without knowing the role would "be dealing with me, one to one."

He fought with almost everyone worth fighting with: the priest channel, the Sunday-raid planners, and above all Divinestorm, in a September feud that produced the officer chat's most profane sentence. The thing about his criticism is that it was mostly right. The split-run chaos was real, the communication gaps were real, the members left in the dark were real. On 24 September 2020, undermined once too often on healer decisions, he quit live in the channel ("Leadership's going to run this guild into the ground, I'm out before it gets much worse") and took his alts with him. The officers restructured their entire chat within the hour. In a sense, that was his last accepted proposal.

panadin.name: Panadin
panadin.html:
Panadin was a paladin from the original friend group and the quieter half of Sleep's Eye of Sulfuras argument. By 27 March 2020 he had gathered all fifty Arcanite Bars for a Sulfuron Hammer. Artimis warned him that Thepaladin was fighting hard for the first Eye and asked what a guaranteed second drop would mean. Panadin accepted the second place because the other player was raiding more.

The queue flared again after Randyfist returned as paladin leader and announced a Ret switch. Artimis and Ragie held the earlier agreement. Panadin kept playing with the group outside raids too, organizing Among Us evenings through the autumn while Artimis was often busy farming AQ consumables or joining a pug.

pawsz.name: Pawsz
pawsz.html:
Pawsz was a druid, a Ninjas officer, and the closest thing the officer chat had to a house intellectual — the one running the numbers on venom sac consumption per Viscidus attempt, proposing member polls with properly phrased questions, and arguing for radical transparency when everyone else wanted PR ("we can just let people read the officer chat. I don't care one bit how it looks"). His one-liners carried more policy than most meetings: "we are not the UN"; "Stoneshield is not something one pops for personal parsing."

He was also the merger's honest observer. It was Pawsz who noted the irony that the supposedly weaker Sleep brought the stricter rules, and Pawsz who refused to let September's departures become a Ninjas-versus- Sleep story: "We are not sat here pointing at Nayla either — why make this about Ninjas and Sleep again?" When the factions finally dissolved into Ascension in December, he was still there, still auditing the decision-making, still allergic to nonsense.

pnats.name: Pnats
pnats.html:
Pnats was a resto druid, Ragie's brother, and the officer chat's conscience. With 144 raids behind him he had the standing to say uncomfortable things, and he used it. When Artimis was benched in December, it was Pnats who opened the debate: the value the man had brought to Sleep and Dusk deserved better. When the officers needed someone to state the hard truth about Glory, he did that too, in words that were kinder in intent than on the page.

He was one of the few constants across all three guilds. He healed Sleep's raids from 2019. The first surviving nomination for a healing-leader role came from Thepaladin on 15 March 2020: "maybe pnats would be good." Pnats became a Dusk officer at the September meeting, worried constantly about healer recruitment ("we lost so many healers"), and kept the loot log honest. He also supplied the archive's comic relief (the discovery that Missdotty was not, in fact, a woman cost him a genuine crisis of confidence) and its most quoted line: on the day Dusk dissolved, he pinged the officers with "BYE DUSK?" and then, at midnight, wrote the era's epitaph: "its been good Sleep > Dusk > Ascension, we've done it all =)"

He raided on through Ascension's Naxxramas farm into 2021, logged onto his brother's warrior when the roster needed it, and stayed the person people forwarded screenshots to when something dramatic happened — which, in this guild, was often.

proctologist.name: Proctologist
proctologist.html:
Proctologist ran Sleep's mages with a methodical style. He tested whether absent players still read Discord and staged promotions during raids so they would feel meaningful. The class moved with little public drama.

The exception was Divinestorm. In April 2020 Divinestorm challenged the class leadership and took the case directly to Artimis. Proctologist thought he "just realy wants to be CL," but offered to step down if it meant one less problem for the guild. Artimis privately preferred to keep him. The officers chose Divinestorm, making Proctologist's restrained exit the first step in the next guild master's rise.

propalica.name: Propalica
propalica.html:
Propalica was a Ret paladin trying to fit into a roster whose four paladin spots were reserved for healers. He worked shifts around raids, but still watched newer players reach raider rank first despite arriving prepared. His protest was direct: if attendance could never overcome class composition, what message did the rank system send?

The argument with Artimis ranged from Onyxia heads to what loot was for. Artimis said it should go where it helped the guild most. Propalica answered that mechanics and preparation mattered too, especially for a Ret paladin who also healed and dispelled. They did not agree on every premise, but they settled the dispute.

In May work made regular raiding impossible. Propalica asked to be demoted rather than leave the guild planning around him. Artimis thanked him for being the first person to say so instead of simply disappearing.

ragie.name: Ragie
ragie.html:
Ragie, Jack on Discord and Pnats's brother, was the guild's tank spine across every era. Exclus referred him on 23 October 2019 as "a really good tank," before Ragie's first logged raid. He inherited the main-tank mantle when Kugel vanished in early 2020, and from then on the records rarely show a serious raid without him. An outside healer sent Sleep a tank-switch video during the first BWL week; Ragie turned the advice into positioning, then crafted the Dark Iron pieces that got the tanks through Firemaw. By the Dusk era he held the formal tank-leader role and ran Sunday raids alongside Jón Snjór.

He is also half of the guild's longest loot argument. What does a main tank deserve first claim on: mitigation gear, crafting materials, a Thunderfury? The question put him repeatedly opposite Glory, whose complaint that "Ragie gets anything he wants" dates to March 2020. The archive is fairer to both men than they were to each other. Ragie's gearing was policy, argued openly in officer channels, and the binding runs that completed Thunderfuries were organised for him and others by name.

He was in the first Four Horsemen kill and the 15/15, made the move to Ascension on migration day (Pnats pinged him to take one last look at the dying Dusk channel), and kept tanking into 2022 in the guild's afterlife.

randyfist.name: Randyfist
randyfist.html:
Randyfist, Randy, Trenfentson on Discord, is one of the archive's quiet constants. He was brought into officer meetings in December 2019 and led the paladins before Thepaladin. Burned out, he stepped away on 2 March 2020 before the planned Nightfall could be crafted for him. He returned in April and accepted the class-leader job again on the 22nd, after Thepaladin lost his account.

The return was not quiet. Eight days into the job he announced a Ret switch and challenged Panadin's Eye of Sulfuras queue, while Artimis and Ragie backed the earlier agreement. A month later Ragie tried to recruit Exclusafk out of Randy's paladin roster and onto a warrior. Randy called it "Warrior Syndrome": the best class, he said, had the worst manners. The disagreement ended without a rupture.

By late Dusk he had become the officer chat's resident hawk. When the December merge talks began, his counsel was piracy: "poach the benched Ascension raiders, cancel the merge, Ascension implodes, we get half their shit. Just like a good ol' divorce." Nobody took the advice. Everybody quoted it.

rockafella.name: Rockafella
rockafella.html:
Rockafella was a warlock and one of the guild's institutionalists. He asked Anders for an Alterac Valley queue bot in December 2019, covered officer meetings for warlock leader Amandil, and later coordinated the class loot with Lyvana. When the mages debated replacing Proctologist, Rockafella gave Divinestorm the strongest peer endorsement: he had "always been wondering why he wasnt the Class Leader from the beginning."

In Dusk he was the voice that said the quiet part about governance out loud: "Class leaders think they are officers. If the class leaders could shut their mouths and run their class and let the officers manage the guild, we wouldn't have this shit." Within the hour, the officers split the chat in two. Few messages in the archive changed more structure faster.

He shows up wherever the record needs a witness with standing: talking Nayla's case through with Divinestorm and establishing that the infamous AQ20 "ninja pull" was a hearthstone misunderstanding; holding the line in the Band of Accuria fight ("we're trying to move away from a culture where the one who shouts loudest is right"); and tanking in the first Four Horsemen kill. He wanted a guild run by its officers, and mostly, after September, he got one.

During the December collapse he kept mailing alchemy materials to the benched Artimis. At 23:31 on migration night, while Dusk disappeared around them, Rockafella was still asking whether Anders could make two flasks.

snjór.name: Snjór
snjór.html:
Jón Snjór, Snjór in the raid and Fantur on his warrior alt, came from Iceland with the Ninjas, held their raid leadership, and owned the Dusk Discord server itself. His tank career is the guild's clearest document of what off-tanking actually cost in Classic. Asked to hold Twin Emperors on a second-string gear set, he laid out the math (5,000 gold of Edgemaster's, double consumables, 5,900 health against 5,000-damage strikes) and then delivered the year's most quietly devastating line: "I've been saying this for weeks, and the answer was like, yeah, we can get someone else to do it."

He led Sunday raids, recruited half the server's strays, took responsibility for things that weren't his fault ("I told them to direct their anger at me"), and became the center of the era's worst day when Yeat kicked him on 30 September and he retaliated through his alt's rank. That kick is the one act the record can't soften, and the one he was restored from within a day once Divinestorm untangled the accusations. His summary of guild philosophy outlived all of it: "the mentality we set in Ninjas was always entertainment before some purple pixels."

supplier.name: Supplier
supplier.html:
Supplier earned his name. Across three years and nearly a thousand messages with Artimis, he was the guild's consumables economy in human form: flasks, protection potions, world-buff logistics, the LBRS venom-sack supply chain that made Viscidus killable. If a raid had what it needed, odds are Supplier had something to do with it.

He was Norwegian, precise, and allergic to sloppy thinking. He asked what a poll was actually for before letting anyone run it. He told his fellow priests exactly how their channel would be run ("take it up with me directly"), and he de-escalated the guild's worst arguments by explaining what an expression had actually meant in context. He was named Healing Officer at the September 2020 meeting and stayed in that seat through the December merge.

Two footnotes belong to him. His dry one-liner "Shosanna was the only priest that got an item yesterday, fyi" became the last straw in Orish's dramatic exit; his whole reaction to the fallout was "Allright, nice to meet ya". And in May 2021 he posted the "Dusk list": a set of tribute video links, one per guildmate, the closest thing the guild ever made to its own memorial before this site.

thepaladin.name: Thepaladin
thepaladin.html:
Thepaladin, Durm on Discord, was Sleep's paladin class leader for six weeks in the spring of 2020, and his 232-message thread with Artimis is one of the archive's richest seams. He was rich (the guild leader once asked, half in awe, where all the money came from), an alchemist, and the owner of the guild's first Sulfuron Hammer, forged by Glory, which put him first in line for the Eye of Sulfuras. Then Panadin got a hammer too, the rule became "everyone with the hammer rolls," and Durm's protest ("That doesnt make me happy ... Retadin mainspec tho and was first and so on") is the purest specimen of the guild's endless argument between earned priority and equal chance.

He got the class-leader job on 5 March ("It's your job now :p") and spent it designing debuff priorities and Lok'amir queues. He also bought a Nightfall after the officers had rejected funding a second one, then confessed that it had been sitting in his bags for a week. Sleep tested it in Molten Core on 15 March. The uptime was poor, Thepaladin did about 200 damage per second, and Artimis concluded a regular damage dealer would do 300. The legendary experiment lost to the spreadsheet.

The four paladin raid spots were all healers, which left Ret players arguing for a path into the roster. Thepaladin fought hard for first place in the Eye queue and won it after Panadin accepted the second Eye. Then he lost everything to a hacker in mid-April. Someone logged into his account, the tickets went nowhere, and the thief even quit the guild on his character while Luivi and Shakey watched. Exclusafk covered the class temporarily. His raid log simply stops on 8 April 2020, mid-story. More Classic careers ended his way than any other: not in drama, in a support queue.

tsakimo.name: Tsakimo
tsakimo.html:
Tsakimo's first raid was BWL on 26 February 2020. His connection failed, the raid replaced him, and Anders apologized for not waiting longer. "Dont worry bro im chill person," Tsakimo answered. It was his first raid anywhere, and he liked that Sleep explained what to do. He was promoted to raider on 18 March.

The calm had limits. In July the new rogue leader Twx replaced Kodf's round-robin system with performance loot. Tsakimo could not match the world-buff demands around work and family, so he quit on the 23rd. Divinestorm quietly recruited him back before Dusk formed. On 19 August, the first Dusk AQ40 night, Tsakimo asked for spreadsheet access and resumed recording loot. By November his message had changed to "parse time 99."

He ran the Wednesday rogues through the Dusk era, working the queue with Antzi across the two teams. His class-leader philosophy was transactional in the best sense: "loot is the reward, you make the effort, you focus, you pay for consumables, then you get loot." He handled the Nayla telephone-game with more patience than it deserved ("I will not take part in the insanity") and got a taste of the job's real burden when a relayed conversation turned out to have two versions. "Now you can feel how it's working," Luivi told him, and he laughed.

He was blunt about standards (sign up by Friday or lose your spot, "no exceptions") and blunt about himself, always discounting his own parses before anyone else could. The rogues under him stayed drama-free, which was the only metric he cared about.

twx.name: Twx
twx.html:
Twx joined Sleep in July 2020 with three raids behind him and a clear idea of how rogues should work. Seniority would not matter. Parses, world buffs, the right spec, and consumables would decide loot. Anders warned that Sleep was not a hardcore guild, then gave class leaders room to run their own class. Twx accepted the job on 13 July.

The experiment lasted about three weeks. Twx awarded himself two tier pieces, put sword rogues first, and told the class that better performers would receive priority. Tsakimo left over the system. Ntekapaz brought the complaints to Anders, who checked the performance claim against the logs and wished aloud for someone who could restore Kodf's queues.

Twx also pursued a Thunderfury, at one point planning to buy a Binding from a pug for 5,000 gold. He later claimed to own one already, but the officers never verified it. By the time Dusk formed he was gone, leaving behind the shortest and sharpest class-leader era in Sleep's record.

ulfhild.name: Ulfhild
ulfhild.html:
Ulfhild was the guild's best hunter and made no apology for what that took: world buffs, full consumables, and total focus, every raid, for a character whose job was the damage meter. The Thursday team built its expectations around him, and he delivered so consistently that his one famous lapse became a governance crisis: on 17 September 2020, when a botched pull at the Ahn'Qiraj entrance wasted the buffs he'd spent hours collecting, he quit the raid on the spot.

The three-day officer argument that followed used his name as shorthand for a whole worldview. His defenders — and they were loud — pointed out that a near-perfect raider had been failed by the raid, not the other way around; his critics said no one player's buffs outweigh thirty-nine people's evening. He apologized in private, was back the next week, and kept doing what he always did: pulling, as one officer put it, more than his share. If everyone had pumped like Ulfhild, the mage leader mused that autumn, AQ would take forty-five minutes.

yeat.name: Yeat
yeat.html:
Yeat was the Thursday team's raid leader and master looter — the warrior who actually ran the nights, kept the loot in his bags between raids (occasionally to the guild banker's despair), and dialed in from work trips with lines like "please make preparations as if I'm not there." His raid-leading philosophy hardened after the September pull crisis: stricter comms, less fun on the mic, "I don't want that in my raid, full stop."

His name is attached to the era's strangest day. On 30 September 2020 he kicked Jón Snjór from the guild without consulting anyone — entangled in an accusation Divinestorm privately doubted — and the retaliation and protest quits that followed nearly cracked the guild. The reform that came out of it restricted kick powers for good. Yet the same record shows why he held the job: steady on loot fairness, first to volunteer for unglamorous logistics, and holder of the in-game guild-master character during the transition — which is how a mid-conflict kick became constitutionally possible in the first place.

zados.name: Zados
zados.html:
Zados was the guild's other half of the hunter brain trust and its co-leader in everything but title. From late 2019 onward he shows up wherever decisions were made: running the hunter class and its loot queues, keeping the debuff-slot priority list current, arguing rules in the officer chat with a debater's stamina, and organising the three-week hunter rotation that he, Artimis and Nereb shared when spots got scarce. His pet did enough damage to become a running joke in feral-druid comparisons.

The Dusk era slowly squeezed the old Sleep leadership out of power, and Zados felt it first. In the September 2020 server reshuffle his admin rights were flagged for removal, and when Divinestorm deleted a channel he liked, his reply (that he supposed he wasn't an officer any more, so whatever) is the driest line in the whole archive. He kept working anyway: the debuff documentation, hunter loot calls, and the long Discord-ping culture war he fought on pure principle ("I'm completely basing my reasoning on logic").

In December he was in the room for everything: skeptical of the new partners ("I have a pretty bad impression of ascension players so far"), blunt about roster choices, and finally the one who answered "when are we leaving and merging?" with "today would be good." He was in the first Four Horsemen kill and the Kel'Thuzad clear — one of the few who was there from the first Molten Core to the last boss of Classic.

zhèna.name: Zhèna
zhèna.html:
Zhèna was Jørgen from Nittedal, a warrior who kept ending up in front of the boss when nobody else could. He became a full member on 16 February 2020 and stepped up as temporary main tank in the gap Kugel left. By July the Thunderfury plan had him next for a right-hand Binding after Glory and Ragie. He was still the tank the Thursday team missed months later, when a busy Wednesday forced an undergeared Jón Snjór in front of the Twin Emperors. Fnats named him among the players who most deserved the Drake Fang Talisman: "top of the meters constantly, with attendance, consumables, world buffs."

He was also one of the guild's top damage dealers whenever he wasn't tanking, a two-hander enthusiast, and part of the Nittedal thread that runs through the whole story: his DM transcript with Anders covers BWL preparation, binding-queue politics, and the ordinary friendship underneath ("I bought Diablo 4. I should never have done that," a later message confesses, from another game and another decade of the same crew).
